title: How Solar Became the World's Cheapest Energy Source
paragraphs: Not long ago, solar power was considered an expensive technology, used mainly in special situations such as powering satellites. Today, however, it is one of the cheapest ways to generate electricity. According to the International Energy Agency, for projects with low-cost financing in places with plenty of sunshine, solar is now the cheapest source of electricity in history. So how did this happen?

The answer lies in a dramatic fall in the price of solar panels. According to the research website Our World in Data, solar modules cost about $106 per watt of capacity in 1976, adjusted for inflation. Since then, the price has fallen to just $0.38 per watt, a decline of more than 99%. The cost of the electricity produced by large solar plants has also plunged. Between 2010 and 2019, it fell by 89%. In comparison, the cost of electricity from new coal plants barely changed during that period.

A key reason for this is a pattern known as a "learning curve." As more solar panels are produced, manufacturers learn how to make them more efficiently, which lowers prices. Lower prices then lead to more demand, which in turn leads to even more production. For solar panels, the price has fallen by about 20% every time the total amount of installed capacity around the world has doubled.

This cycle needed a push to get started. In the early days, solar panels were mainly used for niche purposes, such as satellites. Later, government policies and subsidies in countries including the United States, Japan, Germany and China helped to increase demand.

Solar also has another important advantage. Unlike coal and gas power plants, solar farms do not need to buy fuel, and they are relatively cheap to operate. As a result, the cost of solar power depends mainly on the cost of the technology itself. In contrast, fuel makes up around 40% of the cost of electricity from coal, which limits how cheap it can become.

Nevertheless, fossil fuels still supply about 79% of the world's energy. However, as costs continue to fall, renewable energy is growing quickly. In 2019, renewables made up 72% of all new power capacity added worldwide.
